rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.1, 3 and Table 4 - the authors build and test their own decision-tree/NSGA-II model on 228,855 daily hydrant observations from Sector II of the Canal del Zujar Irrigation District (2015), reporting confusion matrices for three optimal trees (68-100% of positive and 93-100% of negative irrigation events correctly predicted).
rows.notes: The study's own result is the accuracy of predicting whether a farmer will irrigate on a given day (binary classification of irrigation event occurrence). It does not measure or model any reduction in water loss, water use or energy consumption; the statements in the Conclusions that knowing events one day ahead could optimise pumping-station operation and reduce energy cost are assertions of potential, not results. The claimed effect (water/energy conservation through better coordination of scheduling) is therefore only a downstream possibility of what the study demonstrates (prediction of events), so Q2 is no and upstream is set. Note also that the model predicts when farmers choose to irrigate for district managers rather than advising farmers when to irrigate, so its fit to 'app_scheduling' is loose, though not a clear technology mismatch. Single district, single season, no dispersion measures reported for the accuracy results; the authors note the class-imbalance limitation of CT2/CT3, but this concerns prediction accuracy, not the claimed water-conservation effect.

notes: Full text appears complete (post-print with tables and figure captions). The study is a methodological/predictive modelling paper validated against observed hydrant flow data; it contains no water-saving or energy-saving measurement.
